title: Ki Teitzei: the mother bird (Deuteronomy 22:6–7)
hookLine: send the mother bird away before taking the eggs, a command that promises long life

lines: KI TEITZEI: WHEN YOU GO OUT.
cards: You're walking along a road, and there's a bird's nest in a tree or on the ground, the mother sitting on the eggs or the chicks. It's the kind of moment that lasts a few seconds. The Torah stops for it.
It's in the new portion, Ki Teitzei, when you go out, and the portion is packed.

The medieval Sefer HaChinuch counts seventy-four commandments in it, more than in any other portion: marriage, debts, lost property, fences, wages, animals. And tucked among them, this small scene by the road.

teach.b: The law: don't take the mother along with the young. Send the mother away first, and then you may take the eggs or the chicks.
And the reward, in the old Jewish translation: "that it may be well with thee, and that thou mayest prolong thy days."

teach.h: THE SAME REWARD AS HONORING PARENTS.
teach.b: The Ten Commandments attach the same promise to honoring your father and mother. A weighty family duty and a bird's nest by the road, both rewarded with long days. Why this law?
Here the tradition doesn't speak with one voice.
Maimonides, in his Guide for the Perplexed, says it's about compassion: animals feel grief, a mother bird's distress at seeing her young taken is real, and the Torah wants to spare her.
Nachmanides says it's about us: the law trains people not to become cruel. But the Mishnah, in tractate Berakhot, has a surprise.
If a prayer leader says to God, your mercy reaches even to the bird's nest, they silence him. The Talmud explains: he turns God's commandments into mercy, when they are decrees.
In this reading, no one should claim to know exactly why God commanded it. It's kept because it's commanded.
So one camp says the reason is compassion, another says don't presume a reason at all.
Both camps send the mother away. And maybe that's the point of a tiny law with an enormous reward: the smallest act of care counts.

how: Shiluach haken, sending away the mother bird, is still practiced by some Jews, who seek out a nest of a kosher wild bird to fulfill it, and the debate over its reason is a classic of Jewish thought.

practice: Think of the creatures you'll cross paths with today: a pet who wants attention, a spider in the bathtub, birds at a feeder, the ant on the counter.
Picture one of them, and a gentler way of meeting it than usual, like carrying the spider outside or leaving water out. Small: that's the scale of this law.
